newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrians flock to far-right fold in Euro poll.
newsitem.headline: Austrians flock to far-right fold in Euro poll.

text.p: Austrian voters, stung by sharp budget cuts designed to prepare the country for Europe's single currency, flocked to the fold of the far right on Sunday and dealt a crushing blow to the ruling Social Democrats.

Computer projections after the country's first European parliament elections showed the Freedom Party scoring a record high and consolidating its position as the European Union's most successful nationalist party. The party campaigned strongly against greater European integration.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats suffered their worst result in a nationwide poll since Austria first embraced democracy in 1918.
"This great result is an historic step for us," triumphant far-right leader Joerg Haider said in a first reaction to his party's 28 percent showing.
The Freedom Party scored 6.3 points higher than last December's general election and became the most popular party for the first time in three of the country's nine provinces.
Haider predicted a new pact between conservative parties in the European Parliament by the end of the year to fight against the Maastricht treaty on closer EU integration.

He vowed his party would be headed for victory in the country's next general election in 1999 unless Vranitzky stepped down. "If the government doesn't change its policies, it will meet its Waterloo at the next election," he said.
But a defiant Vranitzky dismissed suggestions his coalition with the conservative People's Party should change course, blaming low turnout for his party's 29.3 percent score.
"This is a clear defeat," he told Austrian television. "But I do not see this result as a call by the electorate to change the composition of the government."
Austrian television said voter turnout was 68 percent, far below the usual participation in national polls.
While acknowledging that voters had sent a protest over the introduction in March of a two-year austerity budget, Vranitzky said Austria had no choice but to remain inside the EU.
"I will not change the policies I believe are correct," he said. "Joining the EU was the right decision."

Austria joined the European bloc 22 months ago following a referendum in which two-thirds of voters backed membership. But Austrians have turned their wrath on the EU, blaming membership for a series of economic ills, welfare cuts and tax hikes.
Anger has risen over Austria's annual net contributions to the EU of 15 billion schillings ($1.4 billion), mounting job losses and rising insolvencies amid a general economic slump.
With 80 percent of the vote counted, projections had the People's Party (OeVP), Vranitzky's junior coalition partner, inching ahead of the Social Democrats with 29.5 percent.
OeVP leader and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel hailed his party's result as its best showing in more than 30 years.
Social Democrat backing plummeted 8.5 points from last December's score of 38 percent.
The party lost one seat to take a total of seven of the 21 seats allocated to Austria in Strasbourg's European Parliament.
The conservatives gained one to hold seven as well. The far right gained one to hold six seats, while the leftist Greens held on to their one seat, projections showed.

The beleaguered Social Democrats also lost their hold on Vienna city hall for the first time since the end of World War Two in a separate election for the country's most powerful regional assembly and will be forced to enter coalition talks.
